newsitem.title: USA: Key lawmakers want to change Medicare means-test plan.
newsitem.headline: Key lawmakers want to change Medicare means-test plan.

text.p: Key senators Monday backed off a controversial plan to make wealthier Medicare recipients pay more for doctors' care, pushing instead to make affluent seniors pay higher monthly premiums.

Both approaches are highly controversial, but the first was criticized as a "sick tax" that would have mainly affected those with medical problems. Sponsors said the premium plan was more equitable because it was based only on income.

As Congress began debate on massive budget legislation, its own analysts also estimated both the House and Senate measures, designed to expand care to as many as 5 million uninsured children, would reach only about 500,000 a year.

Congressional aides said senators had decided they did not have enough support for their original Medicare plan, which for the first time would have made wealthy seniors meet higher deductibles before Part B doctor's coverage kicked in.
Their alternative, which could be debated as early as Tuesday in the Senate, would increase the monthly $43.80 Medicare premium for well-off seniors.

"I do not believe this challenges the Medicare system. I do not believe it's a slippery slope to destryoing Medicare," said Nebraska Democratic Sen. Bob Kerrey, saying low-income Americans should not pay taxes to subsidize affluent seniors.

Kerrey said he agreed to change the bill because of confusion about the deductible plan. The White House did not want the plan included in the budget bill and said it would be difficult to administer.
The idea of tying Medicare coverage to income is highly controversial and it was unclear whether the lawmakers would have the votes for the premium alternative.
"I'm opposed to both," said Massachusetts Democratic Sen. Edward Kennedy, vowing to fight such proposals on the floor.
The Senate opened debate on legislation cutting Medicare by $115 billion and Medicaid by about $13.6 billion.

The measure, and a companion House bill, also include $16 billion for children's health insurance and about $10 billion to restore cuts in welfare. The bills are needed to implement a five-year budget deal between Congress and the White House.
Aside from the deductible, fights are expected over Senate provisions raising the Medicare eligibility age to 67 from 65 and charging seniors $5 for home health visits.
Medicare Part B is voluntary, but nearly all eligible seniors choose it as it covers doctor, laboratory, outpatient hospital and other services not provided by regular Medicare.

The current deductible is $100 per year and the monthly premium is $43.80. Seniors' monthly payment reflects only a quarter of the actual program cost. The federal government subsidizes the remaining 75 percent.
Under the original Senate bill, seniors with incomes $50,000 and above and couples with incomes $75,000 and above would have faced sharply higher out-of-pocket costs.
The deductible would have risen to about $500 a year at the $50,000/$75,000 income level, climbing to about $2,000 for individuals making more than $100,000 and couples making more than $125,000.

Under the amendment, the federal premium subsidy would diminish based on income. The phase-out would begin at $50,000/$75,000 and end at $100,000/$125,000. Seniors in the highest income bracket would pay about $2,160 in premiums.

On children's health, both the House and Senate bills would give states the option of block grants to design their own insurance programs. Republicans said the goal was to cover up to half the nation's 10 million uninsured children.
The CBO estimated the number of newly insured children under either bill would be about 500,000 a year.
In analyzing the House bill, the budget office said governors would spend part of the money on direct health services or to make up for federal cuts in Medicaid.

White House officials and Republicans said they believed the CBO was greatly underestimating the number of children who would be covered. The liberal Center on Budget and Policy Priorities forecast states would use the majority of the funds in later years to replace planned cuts in the Medicaid.

"The children's health money should not be robbed," said Marian Wright Edelman, executive director of the Children's Defense Fund. "This is not there for governors to solve all their other kinds of state problems."
